review.material: The official syllabus page was read in full. The course landing page and existing lecture-note inventory were inspected; individual guest lectures and linked readings were not treated as Knight-authored texts.
review.limitations: This guide describes the public teaching framework, not the contents or effectiveness of the entire course.

evidence.description: Official primary account of the subject’s aims and organization.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: This public MIT OCW collection introduces varied approaches to computation and design. The syllabus includes computing performed both by machine and by hand, and treats design broadly: activities, designers, artifacts and the environments where design happens.

sections.title: The organizing question
sections.text: Which metaphors shape the way we think about computation? Knight asks how a familiar domain helps people understand an abstract one, while making some possibilities visible and marginalizing others.

sections.title: How the subject approaches it
sections.text: The semester is organized into thematic modules with guest faculty speakers, readings and team-based assignments. The stated aim is critical awareness of computational design beyond a particular technique or software tool.

sections.title: What this source establishes
sections.text: The syllabus documents an intellectual framework and teaching plan. It does not report research participants, experimental results or evidence that a specific tool is best. Guest lectures retain their individual authorship.

sections.title: What was not read
sections.text: This review does not cover every lecture PDF or external reading. Their detailed claims and reuse conditions must be checked individually; the course-wide open license does not automatically apply to every linked work.

sections.title: How to read it actively
sections.text: Choose a computational method you already use and name the metaphor behind it: language, machine, growth, conversation or another model. Write what the metaphor makes easy to describe and what it leaves difficult to see. This is a suggested reflection based on the syllabus’s purpose.
